title: 2 Chronicles 16:1–10
context: In Asa’s thirty-sixth year, Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah to block access to Judah. Asa sends silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries to Ben Hadad of Syria to break his treaty with Baasha; Ben Hadad attacks northern Israel, and Baasha stops building. Asa uses Ramah’s materials to build Geba and Mizpah. Hanani the seer rebukes Asa for relying on Syria instead of the LORD, reminding him of the victory over the Ethiopians and Lubim, and declares that he will have wars from then on. Asa imprisons Hanani in anger and oppresses some of the people. The parallel to 16:1–6 is 1 Kings 15:16–22; the rebuke is not in Kings. The date in 16:1 is difficult to fit with Kings’ regnal figures for Baasha (1 Kings 15:33; 16:8), and the difference is noted rather than resolved.

verses.text: In the thirty-sixth year of Asa’s reign, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah, and built Ramah, that he might not allow anyone to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: In Asa’s thirty-sixth year, Baasha builds Ramah to block access to Judah. Arminian readers note that Kings dates Baasha’s reign as ending before this (1 Kings 15:33; 16:8); the difference is named, not resolved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that interpreters propose different ways of reckoning the date, as the 1 Kings 15 notes mention. Both traditions read the verse as the start of a crisis that tests Asa’s trust, while Ramah’s site is generally placed north of Jerusalem.

verses.text: Then Asa brought out silver and gold out of the treasures of the LORD’s house and of the king’s house, and sent to Ben Hadad king of Syria, who lived at Damascus, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Asa sends silver and gold from the temple and palace to Ben Hadad of Syria. Arminian readers note that Asa now turns to a foreign king, using the treasures of God’s house to buy help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers set this beside 14:11, where Asa said no one but the LORD could help. The wording follows 1 Kings 15:18, and for both traditions the payment marks the moment Asa’s trust shifts.

verses.text: “Let there be a treaty between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I have sent you silver and gold. Go, break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, that he may depart from me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Asa asks Ben Hadad to break his treaty with Baasha. Arminian readers note that Asa encourages a foreign king to break his word, a choice the prophet will soon condemn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the request as reliance on political alliance rather than on the LORD. Both traditions read the verse as parallel to 1 Kings 15:19, with nearly identical wording.

verses.text: Ben Hadad listened to King Asa, and sent the captains of his armies against the cities of Israel; and they struck Ijon, Dan, Abel Maim, and all the storage cities of Naphtali.
verses.arminianNotes: Ben Hadad attacks Ijon, Dan, Abel Maim, and the storage cities of Naphtali. Arminian readers note that 1 Kings 15:20 has Abel Beth Maacah and Chinneroth; the differences are named rather than resolved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the strategy succeeding in the short term, though Hanani will reveal its cost. Shared ground: the exact sites of Ijon and Abel Maim are uncertain, and both traditions read the verse as narrative.

verses.text: When Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and let his work cease.
verses.arminianNotes: Baasha stops building Ramah. Arminian readers note that Asa’s plan works, at least for the moment, relieving the immediate pressure on Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see apparent success that masks a deeper failure of trust. Both traditions read the verse as parallel to 1 Kings 15:21, setting up Hanani’s rebuke of what seemed a wise policy.

verses.text: Then Asa the king took all Judah, and they carried away the stones and timber of Ramah, with which Baasha had built; and he built Geba and Mizpah with them.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa takes Ramah’s stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah. Arminian readers note the practical use of the abandoned materials to strengthen Judah’s own border.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Asa securing his frontier by human means. Shared ground: the verse parallels 1 Kings 15:22, and the locations of Geba and Mizpah, both in Benjamin, are generally known but debated in detail.

verses.text: At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said to him, “Because you have relied on the king of Syria, and have not relied on the LORD your God, therefore the army of the king of Syria has escaped out of your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Hanani the seer tells Asa that because he relied on Syria rather than the LORD, Syria’s army has escaped him. Arminian readers see a real failure of trust, rebuked by God’s prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the seer exposing the irony that the treaty cost Asa a victory he might have had. On this point the traditions do not divide: trusting God is honored and leaning on human power is judged.

verses.text: Weren’t the Ethiopians and the Lubim a huge army, with chariots and exceedingly many horsemen? Yet, because you relied on the LORD, he delivered them into your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Hanani recalls the huge army of Ethiopians and Lubim, delivered into Asa’s hand when he relied on the LORD. Arminian readers note that Asa’s own past should have taught him to trust God again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the reminder as exposing the inconsistency of Asa’s later choice. Both traditions note that the Lubim are often identified with Libyans, though this is not certain, and that this detail is not mentioned in chapter 14.

verses.text: For the LORD’s eyes run back and forth throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. You have done foolishly in this; for from now on you will have wars.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s eyes run throughout the earth to show Himself strong for those whose heart is perfect toward Him. Arminian readers see God actively watching and ready to help those who trust Him wholeheartedly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s watchful providence over all the earth. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as fully agreed comfort and warning, compare Zechariah 4:10 by reference; Asa’s foolishness brings wars from now on.

verses.text: Then Asa was angry with the seer, and put him in the prison; for he was in a rage with him because of this thing. Asa oppressed some of the people at the same time.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa angrily imprisons Hanani and oppresses some of the people. Arminian readers state the facts soberly, noting that the king who once welcomed a prophet’s word now punishes a prophet for speaking truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the hardening that can follow a refusal to accept rebuke. Both traditions read the verse as a sad turn in Asa’s story, reported as narrative without minimizing the wrong done.
